13.11 Solutions to Exercises 11 - Exercises on abelian groups Solution. (Question 11.4.1) Let 𝜃 ∶ 𝐺 × 𝐻 → 𝐻 × 𝐺 be the map 𝜃((𝑔, ℎ)) = (ℎ, 𝑔). We must check that 𝜃 is one-to-one, onto and a homomorphism. Choose two elements (𝑔1, ℎ1) and (𝑔2, ℎ2) in 𝐺×𝐻 and recall that (𝑔1, ℎ1)(𝑔2, ℎ2) = (𝑔1𝑔2, ℎ1ℎ2). • (𝜃 is a homomorphism.) First we find 𝜃((𝑔1, ℎ1)(𝑔2, ℎ2)) = 𝜃((𝑔1𝑔2, ℎ1ℎ2)) = (ℎ1ℎ2, 𝑔1𝑔2). Second we find 𝜃((𝑔1, ℎ1))𝜃((𝑔2, ℎ2)) = (ℎ1, 𝑔1)(ℎ2, 𝑔2) = (ℎ1ℎ2, 𝑔1𝑔2). Therefore, 𝜃((𝑔1, ℎ1)(𝑔2, ℎ2)) = 𝜃((𝑔1, ℎ1))𝜃((𝑔2, ℎ2)) and 𝜃 is a homomorphism. • (𝜃 is one-to-one.) If 𝜃((𝑔1, ℎ1)) = 𝜃((𝑔2, ℎ2)) then (ℎ1, 𝑔1) = (ℎ2, 𝑔2), and thus ℎ1 = ℎ2 and 𝑔1 = 𝑔2. We therefore have (𝑔1, ℎ1) = (𝑔2, ℎ2). • (𝜃 is onto.) Any (ℎ, 𝑔) ∈ 𝐻 × 𝐺 satisfies (ℎ, 𝑔) = 𝜃((𝑔, ℎ)). Solution. (Question 11.4.2) Here we use the Quick Subgroup Test. • Identity: Now 𝐾 ≤ 𝐺 so 𝑒𝐺 ∈ 𝐾 and similarly 𝑒𝐻 ∈ 𝐽 . Therefore (𝑒𝐺, 𝑒𝐻) ∈ 𝐾 × 𝐽 and (𝑒𝐺, 𝑒𝐻) is the identity of 𝐺 × 𝐻. • Inverse: If (𝑔, ℎ) ∈ 𝐾 × 𝐽 , then 𝑔 ∈ 𝐾 and ℎ ∈ 𝐽 and therefore (because 𝐾 and 𝐽 are groups) 𝑔−1 ∈ 𝐾 and ℎ−1 ∈ 𝐽 . Thus (𝑔−1, ℎ−1) ∈ 𝐾 × 𝐽 . Finally, we check that this is the inverse of (𝑔, ℎ). Indeed it is: (𝑔, ℎ)(𝑔−1, ℎ −1) = (𝑔𝑔−1, ℎℎ −1) = (𝑒𝐺, 𝑒𝐻). • Closure: If (𝑔1, ℎ1) ∈ 𝐾 × 𝐽 and (𝑔2, ℎ2) ∈ 𝐾 × 𝐽 , then (in 𝐺 × 𝐻) we know (𝑔1, ℎ1)(𝑔2, ℎ2) = (𝑔1𝑔2, ℎ1ℎ2) ∈ 𝐺 × 𝐻. Since 𝐾 and 𝐽 are groups, and 𝑔𝑖 ∈ 𝐾 and ℎ𝑖 ∈ 𝐽 , we have 𝑔1𝑔2 ∈ 𝐾 and ℎ1ℎ2 ∈ 𝐽 . Therefore, (𝑔1, ℎ1)(𝑔2, ℎ2) = (𝑔1𝑔2, ℎ1ℎ2) ∈ 𝐾 × 𝐽 . Solution. (Question 11.4.3) The proof roughly follows this plan: we find a cyclic subgroup 𝐻 of 𝐶𝑝𝑟 that has order 𝑝𝑠. Then 𝐻 ≅ 𝐶𝑝𝑠. We will find 𝐻 by finding an element ℎ ∈ 𝐶𝑝𝑟 that has order 𝑝𝑠, and setting 𝐻 = ⟨ℎ⟩. If 𝑠 = 0 or 𝑠 = 𝑟 then there is nothing to prove, so assume 1 ≤ 𝑠 < 𝑟. Let 𝜏 be the 𝑝𝑟-cycle 𝜏 = (1 2 ⋯ 𝑝𝑟). Then 𝐶𝑝𝑟 = ⟨𝜏 ⟩. Set ℎ = 𝜏 𝑟−𝑠. We claim that 𝑜(ℎ) = 𝑝𝑠. Indeed ℎ𝑝𝑠 = (𝜏 𝑝 𝑟−𝑠)𝑝𝑠 = 𝜏 𝑝𝑟−𝑠⋅𝑝𝑠 = 𝜏 𝑝𝑟 = 𝑒. Therefore 𝑜(ℎ) ≤ 𝑝𝑠. On the other hand, 𝑜(ℎ) ≥ 𝑝𝑠 since if 0 < ℓ < 𝑝𝑠 then ℎℓ = 𝜏 𝑝𝑟−𝑠ℓ ≠ 𝑒 because 𝑝𝑟−𝑠ℓ < 𝑝𝑟 = 𝑜(𝜏 ). Thus 𝑜(𝜏 𝑘) = 𝑝𝑠. Finally, we note that 𝐻 = ⟨ℎ⟩ ≤ 𝐶𝑝𝑟 is a cyclic group of order 𝑝𝑠 and is therefore isomorphic to 𝐶𝑝𝑠. 140

(Question 11.4.4) By the Fundamental Theorem of Finite Abelian Groups, every abelian group of order 72 is of the form 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝 𝑒𝑛 𝑛 , where 𝑝1, … , 𝑝𝑛 are (not necessarily distinct) primes and 𝑒1, … , 𝑒𝑛 are natural numbers and 𝑝𝑒1 1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 = 72. Each factorisation is unique up to reordering of the factors (i.e. reordering factors doesn’t matter, but different factorisations result in non-isomorphic groups). Therefore we can find, up to isomorphism, all abelian groups of order 72 = 2 3 ⋅ 32 by thinking of all the ways of writing 72 as 𝑝𝑒1 1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 where the 𝑝𝑖 are not necessarily distinct primes. As long as we are systematic about it, this is easy. Remember we don’t care about the order of the primes. (Question 11.4.5) This is true, but it only holds for abelian groups! Here is the proof. By The Fundamental Theorem of Abelian Groups, there are (not necessarily distinct) primes 𝑝1, … , 𝑝𝑛 and natural numbers 𝑒1, … , 𝑒𝑛 such that 𝑝𝑒1 1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 = 𝑚 and 𝐺 ≅ 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 . Notice that, since 𝑝𝑒1 1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 = 𝑚 and 𝑘∣𝑚, the number 𝑘 must also be a product of (some or possibly all of) these primes, so we can write, 𝑘 = 𝑝𝑑1 1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑑𝑛 𝑛 , for some integers 0 ≤ 𝑑𝑖 ≤ 𝑒𝑖 for 𝑖 = 1, … , 𝑛. For each 𝑖 ∈ {1, … , 𝑛} we can use Question 11.4.3 to deduce that 𝐶 𝑝𝑑𝑖 𝑖 ≲ 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑖 𝑖 . Therefore by Question 11.4.2, 𝐶𝑝𝑑1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑑𝑛 𝑛 ≲ 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑛 𝑛 ≅ 𝐺. Since 𝐶𝑝𝑑1 1 × ⋯ × 𝐶 𝑝𝑑𝑛 𝑛 has order 𝑝𝑑1 1 ⋯ 𝑝𝑑𝑛 𝑛 = 𝑘, it follows that 𝐺 has a subgroup of order 𝑘. 141
